title: Installing Node.js
idea: Setting up Node.js means installing the runtime once, then checking that your terminal can find `node` and `npm`.
points: This book's examples are verified on Node 20; production needs a supported LTS.
The installer from nodejs.org includes `npm`, the package manager.
A version manager such as `nvm` installs several Node versions and switches between them.

items.label: Install Node
items.text: Run the installer. It adds `node` and `npm` to your terminal.

items.label: Check versions
items.text: Open a new terminal. Each command should print a version number.

items.label: Pick an editor
items.text: Any code editor works. One with a built-in terminal saves switching windows.

items.label: Make a folder
items.text: Give each project its own folder. Commands and files then stay together.

code.title: Check and prepare
code.caption: Typed in a terminal. The first two lines are optional.

walk.text: Optional: `nvm` on macOS or Linux installs a Node version and switches to it.
Print both versions. If `node` is not found, open a new terminal and retry.
Create a project folder and move into it. Your files and commands live here.

pitfalls: Open a new terminal after installing; an old one may not find `node`.
Avoid `sudo` with `npm`; a version manager prevents permission errors.
Run production on a supported LTS release; old versions stop receiving security fixes.

quiz.q: Which command prints the Node version you installed?
quiz.why: `node --version` asks the `node` program for its version. `npm --version` reports npm, a separate tool.

takeaway: You are ready when `node --version` and `npm --version` both print a version.
